2010B16.goal: A unit square and a circle of radius $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}$ share a centre. The circle pokes out past each side in four equal circular segments. We want their total area.

tools.name: Segment angle
tools.why: $d$ is the distance from the centre to a side; the segment's central angle is $2\theta=60^\circ$.

2010B16.approach: Each side is $\tfrac12$ from the centre, less than $r\approx0.577$, while the corners are $0.707$ away, outside the circle. So the circle sticks out past each side in a segment, with central angle $60^\circ$.
2010B16.bridge: Find the $60^\circ$ segments and add four of them.
solution: Each side is $\tfrac12$ from the centre, giving a $60^\circ$ segment of radius $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}$.
2010B16.shortcut: Circle area minus the part inside the square also works, but segments are direct.
traps: Assuming the corners are inside the circle.
2010B16.recognize: A circle and a polygon with the same centre: the circle sticks out in segments; find each segment's central angle from $\cos\theta=\tfrac dr$.

2010B17.goal: Each school sends $3$ students; Andrea is the median and the best on her team, whose others placed $37$th and $64$th. We want the number of schools $n$. Bounds from her rank pin $n$ down.

tools.name: Inequalities from teammates
tools.why: Andrea beat Beth; Carla's rank exists.

2010B17.approach: $3n$ must be odd (a single median), so $n$ is odd. Andrea's rank $\tfrac{3n+1}2$ is better than $37$, and there are at least $64$ students.

check.q: What is the median rank among $69$ students?

2010B17.bridge: Use the median position, the teammates' ranks, and parity.
solution: Andrea's rank $\tfrac{3n+1}2$ is less than $37$, so $n\le24$.
2010B17.shortcut: Parity of the total decides between the bounds.
traps: Forgetting the median requires an odd number of students.
2010B17.recognize: Ranking problems: translate each statement into an inequality on the total; parity often finishes.

2010B18.goal: $a,b,c$ are random from $1$–$2010$; we want $P(3\mid abc+ab+a)$. Factor out $a$ and work mod $3$ (residues are uniform since $3\mid2010$).
2010B18.approach: Divisible by $3$ iff $3\mid a$ or $b(c+1)\equiv2\pmod3$. Compute the second probability by listing residue pairs.

check.q: What fraction of $1..2010$ are multiples of $3$?
Which pairs of residues multiply to $2\pmod3$?

2010B18.bridge: Factor, then split into $3\mid a$ or the other factor $\equiv0$.
2010B18.shortcut: Factor first; probabilities of "either factor divisible" combine with a complement.
traps: Adding the two cases without the $\tfrac23$ factor.
2010B18.recognize: Divisibility probabilities: factor the expression and use residues.

2010B19.goal: A circle has $r^2=156$; equilateral triangle $ABC$ has $BC$ as a chord, $OA=4\sqrt3$, with $O$ outside the triangle. Both $O$ and $A$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$.

tools.name: Perpendicular bisector
tools.fact: OB=OC,\ AB=AC\Rightarrow O,A\text{ on the bisector of }BC

2010B19.approach: With $M$ the midpoint of $BC$, $OA$ is $OM-AM$ or $OM+AM$ depending on sides. Test the choices; $s=6$ gives $OM=7\sqrt3$, $AM=3\sqrt3$, difference $4\sqrt3$ with $O$ beyond $A$ (outside the triangle).
2010B19.bridge: Put $O$ and $A$ on the bisector of $BC$ and compare distances.
solution: $O$ and $A$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$.
2010B19.shortcut: Solve $\sqrt{156-s^2/4}=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2s+4\sqrt3$ by squaring, or test the choices.
2010B19.recognize: Isosceles/equilateral triangles on a chord: the apex and centre are on the chord's perpendicular bisector.

2010B20.goal: Two circles outside a regular hexagon are tangent to lines $BC$ and $FA$; one also touches $AB$, the other $DE$. We want the ratio of their areas. Lines $BC$ and $FA$ meet at a point $P$, and both circles sit in the same $60^\circ$ angle at $P$.

tools.name: Circle in an angle
tools.fact: \text{centre on the bisector at distance }d\text{ from }P\Rightarrow r=d\sin30^\circ=\tfrac d2
tools.why: Tangent to both sides of a $60^\circ$ angle.

tools.name: Hexagon distances
tools.why: $PAB$ is equilateral with side $1$; the hexagon's height is $\sqrt3$.

2010B20.approach: Take side $1$. $P$ is the apex of the equilateral triangle on $AB$. The first circle is the incircle of $\triangle PAB$. The second is in the same angle but just beyond $DE$, which is $\tfrac{3\sqrt3}2$ from $P$. Use $r=\tfrac d2$ for both.

check.q: What is the inradius of an equilateral triangle with side $1$?

steps.title: Second circle
steps.explain: Its centre is at distance $d$ from $P$ with $r_2=\tfrac d2$, and it touches $DE$ from beyond: $d-r_2=\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}$. So $\tfrac d2=\tfrac{3\sqrt3}2$, $r_2=\tfrac{3\sqrt3}2$.

check.q: If radii are in ratio $9$, areas are in ratio?

2010B20.bridge: Both circles are inscribed in the angle at $P$; compare their distances from $P$.
solution: Lines $BC$ and $FA$ meet at $P$, forming equilateral $\triangle PAB$.
The second circle has $d-\tfrac d2=\tfrac{3\sqrt3}2$, so $r_2=\tfrac{3\sqrt3}2$.
2010B20.shortcut: Circles in the same angle are similar from $P$; the ratio of radii equals the ratio of distances to their tangent lines on the far side.
traps: Placing the second circle between $AB$ and $DE$.
2010B20.recognize: Circles tangent to two fixed lines: they are dilations from the lines' intersection.

2010B21.goal: A random $4$-digit palindrome $abba$; we want $P(7\mid abba)$. Write it as $1001a+110b$ and note $1001=7\cdot11\cdot13$.
2010B21.approach: $7\mid1001a$ always, so we need $7\mid110b$. Since $110\equiv5\pmod7$, that means $7\mid b$: $b\in\{0,7\}$.
2010B21.recognize: Palindromes: expand by place value; factors like $1001$, $11$ appear.

2010B23.goal: Fill a $3\times3$ grid with $1$–$9$ so rows and columns increase. We count such arrays (standard Young tableaux of a $3\times3$ shape).

tools.name: Hook lengths of $3	imes3$
tools.why: Cells to the right plus below plus itself.

2010B23.approach: Use the hook length formula: product of hooks is $5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1=8640$, and $\tfrac{9!}{8640}=42$. (A casework check: $1$ is top-left, $9$ bottom-right, and the centre must be $4$, $5$ or $6$.)

check.q: What is the hook length of the top-left cell?

solution: Hook lengths of the $3\times3$ grid multiply to $8640$.
2010B23.shortcut: Casework on the centre ($4$, $5$ or $6$) gives $12+18+12=42$.
2010B23.recognize: Increasing rows and columns: Young tableaux; use the hook length formula or casework on the centre.

2010B24.goal: Raiders score a geometric sequence $a,ar,ar^2,ar^3$; Wildcats an arithmetic one $a,a+d,a+2d,a+3d$ (same first quarter). Raiders win by $1$, each total at most $100$. We want the first-half total.

tools.name: Totals
tools.why: Raiders total equals Wildcats total plus $1$.

tools.name: Divisibility by 6
tools.why: The left side is a multiple of $6$.

2010B24.approach: Try small ratios. $r=2$: $15a=4a+6d+1$, so $11a=6d+1$; $a=5$, $d=9$ works with totals $75$ and $74$. Other ratios fail divisibility or the $100$ bound.
2010B24.bridge: Set totals equal (plus one), try $r=2$, and add the first-half scores.
2010B24.recognize: Geometric vs arithmetic sequences with integer constraints: test small ratios and use divisibility.

2010B25.goal: An integer-coefficient polynomial equals $a$ at $1,3,5,7$ and $-a$ at $2,4,6,8$. We want the smallest $a>0$. Factor out the known roots of $P(x)-a$ and see what the other values force.

tools.name: Integer coefficients
tools.fact: Q\text{ has integer coefficients, so }Q(k)\in\mathbb Z
tools.why: Dividing by monic factors keeps integer coefficients.

2010B25.approach: At $x=2,4,6,8$: $-2a=(\text{product})\cdot Q(x)$. The products are $-15$, $9$, $-15$, $105$. So $\tfrac{2a}{15}$, $\tfrac{2a}{9}$, $\tfrac{2a}{105}$ must be integers: $a$ is a multiple of $\operatorname{lcm}(9,15,105)=315$.

steps.title: Divisibility
steps.explain: $Q(2)=\tfrac{2a}{15}$, $Q(4)=-\tfrac{2a}{9}$, $Q(8)=-\tfrac{2a}{105}$ must be integers. So $a$ is a multiple of $\operatorname{lcm}(15,9,105)=315$. With $a=315$ the needed values are $Q(2)=42$, $Q(4)=-70$, $Q(6)=42$, $Q(8)=-6$, and $Q(x)=42-56(x-2)+28(x-2)(x-4)-8(x-2)(x-4)(x-6)$ has integer coefficients and hits all four.

2010B25.bridge: Factor $P(x)-a$, evaluate at the even points, and require integer values of $Q$.
2010B25.shortcut: The lcm of the four products' absolute values (ignoring the factor $2$) gives the answer.
traps: Forgetting the factor $2$ in $-2a$ (it does not change the lcm here since the products are odd).
2010B25.recognize: Polynomials with integer coefficients taking given values: factor out known roots; integrality of the quotient constrains parameters.
